item.title: Multifunctional Biodegradable Biobeads for Smart Water Purification Systems
item.description:
Overview

This project presents biodegradable hydrogel bio-beads formulated from natural materials — Moringa seed powder, banana peel powder, orange peel powder, and activated charcoal — encapsulated within a sodium alginate matrix. These beads purify contaminated water through combined coagulation, adsorption, and biosorption mechanisms. A smart monitoring system, built using an ESP32 microcontroller and turbidity sensor, was integrated to evaluate purification performance through real-time turbidity tracking.

The Problem

Conventional water treatment relies heavily on chemical coagulants such as alum and ferric salts. While effective, these chemicals generate harmful sludge, raise treatment costs, and introduce secondary environmental pollution. Natural coagulants like Moringa oleifera offer a sustainable alternative, but their effectiveness is typically assessed through inconsistent manual observation. There is a need for a standardized, biodegradable treatment method paired with objective, real-time performance measurement.

Objectives

  • Develop biodegradable hydrogel bio-beads using natural coagulant and adsorbent materials.
  • Encapsulate these materials within a sodium alginate matrix for stability and controlled interaction with water.
  • Integrate an ESP32-based turbidity monitoring system to quantify purification performance in NTU (Nephelometric Turbidity Unit).
  • Comparatively evaluate different bead formulations for turbidity reduction efficiency.

Working Principle

The system combines two purification mechanisms within a single bead:

  • Coagulation: Moringa seed proteins carry a positive charge and neutralize negatively charged suspended particles, causing them to clump together and settle (floc formation).
  • Adsorption / Biosorption: Banana peel powder, orange peel powder, and activated charcoal contain cellulose, lignin, pectin, and porous carbon structures that trap and bind contaminants.

These materials are held within a sodium alginate hydrogel, formed through ionic cross-linking with calcium chloride — a structure known as the “egg-box model.” This matrix keeps the active materials stable and allowed controlled contact with the water being treated.

System Design

Treatment Module

Bio-beads are introduced into contaminated water, where their embedded materials interact with suspended particles through coagulation, adsorption, biosorption, and chelation — improving water clarity over time.

Monitoring Module

A turbidity sensor connected to an ESP32 microcontroller continuously measures water clarity before and after treatment. Readings are processed and displayed via the serial monitor, with green and red LED indicators providing a simple visual signal of water quality.

Bead Preparation Process

  1. Raw material collection — Moringa seeds, banana peels, orange peels, and charcoal.
  2. De-moisting — Materials washed and naturally dried.
  3. Grinding — Dried materials ground into fine powders.
Moringa Powder Banana Peel Powder
Orange Peel Powder Activated Charcoal
  1. Alginate solution preparation — Sodium alginate dissolved in distilled water (using a double-boiler setup).

Figure 1: Double-boiler setup for dissolving sodium alginate.

  1. Mixing — Powders combined into the alginate solution to form a homogeneous suspension.
  2. Bead formation — Mixture dropped into calcium chloride solution, triggering ionic cross-linking via a syringe.

Figure 2: Dripping biomaterial slurry into Calcium Chloride solution using a syringe.

  1. Washing — Beads rinsed with distilled water to remove impurities.
  2. Drying — Beads dried until stable and ready for use.

Figure 3: Final prepared hydrogel bio-beads.

Materials and Equipment

Hardware

  • ESP32 Development Board
  • Optical Turbidity Sensor Module (Analog)
  • 5V DC Adapter / Power Bank
  • Solderless Breadboard and Jumper Wires
  • Two 10 kΩ Resistors (voltage divider, 5V to 3.3V conversion)
  • Red and Green LED Indicators with 220 Ω Resistors
  • Sodium Alginate-Based Bio-Coagulant Beads
  • Glass Beaker for Water Samples

Software

  • Arduino IDE with ESP32 Board Package
  • C/C++
  • Arduino IDE Serial Monitor

Testing and Results

The system was evaluated across six test cases covering bead formation, treatment efficiency, sensor accuracy, and overall system integration:

  • Bead formation: Beads formed as stable, spherical structures that maintained integrity without disintegration.
  • Treatment efficiency: Contaminated water showed a clear, visible improvement in clarity after treatment.
  • Turbidity sensor: Accurately detected and reported varying turbidity levels across different samples.
  • ESP32 monitoring: Continuously processed and displayed sensor readings without interruption.
  • LED indication: Correctly switched between green (safe turbidity) and red (high turbidity) based on threshold values.
  • Overall system: All components operated together successfully, meeting the project’s intended objectives.
Initial Contaminated Water Treated & Clarified Water
Raw turbid sample before treatment Clear sample after 30 mins treatment
Turbid Water (System Triggered) Purified Water (Target Achieved)
Red LED active during high turbidity Green LED active post-purification

Applications

  • Household water pre-treatment — a simple first step to reduce turbidity before further purification.
  • Rural and remote water treatment — low-cost, community-level purification without dependence on infrastructure.
  • Agricultural and irrigation use — reduces suspended solids in water used for irrigation.
  • Educational and research use — a hands-on tool for studying coagulation, adsorption, and biosorption.
  • Environmental monitoring — real-time turbidity tracking for water bodies.
  • Emergency and disaster relief — a lightweight, portable option for treating water during shortages.
  • Smart water quality systems — combines sustainable purification with IoT-based monitoring.

Portable Bio-Bead Kit Concept

The beads were also designed as a compact, ready-to-use kit — pre-packaged in zip-lock pouches for easy transport and distribution. Requiring no electricity or specialized equipment, the kit is suited for schools, NGOs, and community programs operating in areas with limited infrastructure, offering a low-cost pre-treatment option for water used in irrigation or non-potable applications.

Figure: Pre-packaged portable bio-bead kit (concept visualization, AI-generated).

Limitations and Future Scope

  • Bead composition, porosity, and controlled-release characteristics can be further optimized for improved treatment performance.
  • Additional sensors — pH, Total Dissolved Solids (TDS), dissolved oxygen, temperature, and conductivity — could be integrated for more comprehensive water quality analysis.
  • IoT connectivity could enable remote monitoring and cloud-based data storage.
  • Future work could extend the system to heavy metal removal, wastewater treatment, and community-scale purification.

Relevance to Sustainable Development Goals

  • SDG 3 — Good Health and Well-Being: Reduces exposure to contaminated water and supports healthier living conditions.
  • SDG 6 — Clean Water and Sanitation: Provides an affordable, eco-friendly approach to improving water clarity.
  • SDG 9 — Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure: Combines biotechnology with smart sensing for an innovative treatment approach.
  • SDG 12 — Responsible Consumption and Production: Converts agricultural waste (banana and orange peels) into a value-added product.
  • SDG 13 — Climate Action: Reduces dependence on synthetic chemicals in favor of biodegradable alternatives.

Figure: Sustainable Development Goals alignment collage.

Conclusion

Building this system bridged biotechnology with practical IoT execution, demonstrating that sustainable agricultural waste can directly solve real-world clean water challenges through smart, local engineering.

item.title: Design and Development of a Paper-Based Colorimetric Iron Detection Kit
item.description:
Overview

This project presents a paper-based analytical device (PAD) for detecting iron (Fe³⁺) in water samples. It repurposes a well-established chemical reaction — potassium thiocyanate (KSCN) reacting with ferric ions to form a blood-red complex — into a compact, field-usable format. The device was developed using the Design Thinking (IDT) framework, with a focus on affordability, portability, and accessibility for resource-limited settings.

The Problem

Conventional iron detection methods, such as spectrophotometry and atomic absorption spectroscopy, require expensive instrumentation, trained personnel, and laboratory infrastructure. This makes routine water testing impractical in rural or remote areas. There is a clear need for a simple, low-cost method that delivers fast, visually interpretable results without specialized equipment.

Objectives

  • Design a paper-based sensing platform for iron detection
  • Use potassium thiocyanate as a selective reagent for Fe³⁺
  • Produce a visible colorimetric response proportional to iron concentration
  • Apply Design Thinking principles to create an accessible, scalable solution

Working Principle

The detection method is based on a coordination chemistry reaction:

Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ → [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ (blood-red complex).

The intensity of the red color produced is directly proportional to the concentration of Fe³⁺ in the sample, allowing for semi-quantitative estimation through visual comparison.

Development Process

Empathize & Define

The design process began with identifying the core constraint faced by users in remote regions: no access to laboratory infrastructure or technical training. The problem was defined as the need for a portable, affordable method to detect iron at the point of use.

Ideate

The concept involved converting a conventional liquid-based assay into a solid-state, paper-based format. Potassium thiocyanate was selected for its strong, selective response to Fe³⁺. Whatman filter paper was chosen as the substrate for its capillary action, low cost, and biodegradability.

Prototype

The prototype was developed by creating defined reaction zones on filter paper, impregnating them with potassium thiocyanate, and allowing the reagent to dry and stabilize before testing with iron samples of varying concentrations.

Materials and Equipment

Materials

  • Whatman filter paper (or equivalent substrate)
  • Potassium thiocyanate (KSCN)
  • Standard ferric ion (Fe³⁺) stock solution
  • Distilled water (for dilutions and as a negative control)

Equipment

  • Test tubes or Erlenmeyer flasks (for preparing simulated samples)
  • Dropper or micropipette
  • Tweezers (for handling treated strips)
  • Protective gloves and laboratory glassware

Procedure

Step 1: Prepare Simulated Water Samples

Since real drinking water typically contains very low iron levels, simulated samples were prepared at amplified concentrations to ensure clear, visible color differentiation:

  1. Prepare a Fe³⁺ stock solution of known concentration.
  2. Dilute the stock with distilled water to create three test samples — 5 mg/L (low), 10 mg/L (moderate), and 15 mg/L (high) — and an unrealistic sample (extremely high).
  3. Label each sample clearly (Low, Moderate, High) and keep separate in test tubes or flasks.

Figure: Stimulated samples having low, moderate, high concentrations of iron.

Step 2: Prepare the Reagent-Treated Strip

  1. Impregnate defined zones on the filter paper with KSCN solution.
  2. Allow the strip to dry completely and stabilize before use.

Step 3: Run the Test

  1. Using tweezers, dip a thiocyanate-treated strip into each prepared sample.
  2. Observe the color change on the strip over a few seconds.

Figure: Adding the iron sample using a dropper onto a dried filter paper after treating with KSCN.

  1. Repeat for each concentration, including the unrealistic sample.

Step 4: Interpret Results

  1. Compare the resulting color against a pre-made intensity scale to estimate the iron concentration.
  2. Confirm the gradient — pale orange (low) to deep reddish-orange (high).

Results

The kit produced a clear, consistent colorimetric response across all three simulated samples. The 5 mg/L (low) sample showed a pale orange color, the 10 mg/L (moderate) sample showed a stronger orange-red, and the 15 mg/L (high) sample produced a deep reddish-orange to blood-red color — with the unrealistic sample showing an intense red color. This gradient confirmed the sensitivity and reliability of the sensor across a practical concentration range.

Final Results Gradient Strip Color Indication
Color gradient seen in iron samples Strip color indicating presence of iron

Portable Iron Detection Kit Concept

Beyond the lab-scale prototype, the sensor was also designed with real-world deployment in mind. The kit consists of pre-treated filter paper strips impregnated with potassium thiocyanate reagent, packaged alongside a visual reference chart showing approximate iron concentration in ppm. A user simply applies a water sample to the strip and matches the resulting color against the chart — no equipment, no calibration, no technical training required.

This makes the kit especially suited for on-the-spot testing in rural and low-resource communities, where access to high-tech water analysis is often limited or entirely unavailable. By replacing instrumentation with a simple visual comparison, the kit brings reliable, actionable water safety information directly to the people who need it most — right at the source.

Figure: Pre-packaged portable Iron Detection kit (concept visualization, AI-generated).

Limitations and Future Scope

The current design selectively detects Fe³⁺ and does not account for Fe²⁺ present in a sample. This can be addressed by introducing an oxidizing agent, such as hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), to convert Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ — enabling total iron estimation.

Planned areas for future development:

  • A smartphone-based application to quantify color intensity and provide numerical results
  • Expansion to detect total iron content through oxidation chemistry
  • Scaled production for community-level water testing programs
  • Adaptation of the platform to detect other heavy metals and contaminants

Relevance to Sustainable Development Goals

  • SDG 3 — Good Health and Well-being: Supports safer drinking water through accessible iron monitoring.
  • SDG 6 — Clean Water and Sanitation: Promotes affordable, accessible water quality testing.

Figure: Sustainable Development Goals alignment collage.

Conclusion

This project shows how a well-established laboratory reaction can be reimagined as an accessible, real-world diagnostic tool. By combining chemistry, materials, and a human-centered design process, the iron detection kit offers a practical alternative to conventional testing — one that doesn’t rely on expensive instrumentation or specialized training. It was a valuable exercise in taking core biotechnology concepts and applying them to a genuine gap in accessible water testing.
